topicName: Transactions (MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD) and Lua Scripting
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Transactions and Lua Scripting in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis provides mechanisms to execute multiple commands atomically to ensure data consistency. This tutorial covers Redis transactions using MULTI, EXEC, and DISCARD, as well as atomic script execution via Lua scripting."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Redis Transactions (MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Redis transaction allows a group of commands to be executed in a single isolated step. Transactions are characterized by two crucial guarantees:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"All commands in a transaction are serialized and executed sequentially. A request issued by another client will never be served in the middle of a Redis transaction."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The EXEC command triggers the execution of all commands in the queue. If a client loses connection before EXEC, no commands are executed."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Basic Transaction Workflow"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"To start a transaction, use the MULTI command. Subsequent commands are queued. Calling EXEC runs the queue, while DISCARD flushes the queue and cancels the transaction."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"MULTI
SET account:1:balance 100
SET account:2:balance 200
EXEC"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Handling Errors in Transactions"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike relational databases, Redis transactions do not support rollbacks for runtime errors. If a command fails during EXEC, the other commands in the queue still execute."},{"order":12,"type":"heading","text":"2. Optimistic Locking with WATCH"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis transactions do not support traditional pessimistic locking. Instead, WATCH provides a way to implement optimistic locking (Check-And-Set)."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"WATCH mykey
val = GET mykey
// Compute new value locally
MULTI
SET mykey newval
EXEC"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"If the watched key is modified by another client before EXEC is called, the entire transaction is aborted and EXEC returns a null reply."},{"order":16,"type":"heading","text":"3. Lua Scripting in Redis"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Lua scripting provides a powerful alternative to transactions. Redis executes Lua scripts atomically (similar to a MULTI/EXEC block) and allows complex conditional logic directly on the server side."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Executing Lua Scripts with EVAL"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"The EVAL command takes a script, the number of keys, and the key/argument values. Keys and arguments should be accessed via KEYS and ARGV arrays inside the Lua script."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"EVAL "local current = redis.call('get', KEYS[1])
if current == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call('set', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
else
    return 0
end" 1 mykey oldval newval"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Caching Scripts with EVALSHA"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"To avoid sending large script strings over the network repeatedly, use SCRIPT LOAD to cache the script on the server and execute it using EVALSHA with its SHA1 hash."},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"SCRIPT LOAD "return redis.call('get', KEYS[1])"
EVALSHA "sha1_hash_string" 1 mykey"},{"order":24,"type":"heading","text":"Summary: Transactions vs. Lua"},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use MULTI/EXEC for simple batching of independent commands."},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use WATCH for optimistic locking concurrency control."},{"order":27,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Lua scripts for complex conditional logic, reduced network overhead, and server-side atomicity."}]
